scope: Python DNS worker capacity ownership across object construction, slot acquisition, worker startup, caller cancellation and worker completion. Two local kernel alarms and otherwise controlled handler/error injection with fake DNS resolution; no live remote exploit or deployment test.
changes: Construct the completion event, result container and thread object before reserving resolver capacity.

Record deadline expiry immediately but defer its exception on the main thread during slot acquisition and worker startup, so ownership reaches either a failed-start cleanup or the running worker before cancellation propagates.
A running worker retains its slot until name resolution finishes; caller timeout never releases an in-flight worker slot. Capture the same semaphore instance for acquisition and release.
Preserve public deadline errors, startup failure cleanup, four-slot capacity, main-thread-only timer ownership and literal-address behavior.

baseline.reproduction: Cancellation after a slot was consumed but before a worker could release it stranded capacity. Four repeated interrupted constructors consumed all four slots; the next four attempts failed with capacity exhaustion instead of the injected deadline. Event construction failure also leaked a slot.

checks: Deadline injection during event/thread construction, after semaphore consumption, and before worker handoff preserves capacity.
Ordinary event/thread construction and startup failures leave capacity available.
Real 20 ms SIGALRM timers interrupt delayed thread construction and expire during delayed slot acquisition without stranding capacity.
Expiry after startup or during completion waiting retains the occupied slot until the fake resolver returns successfully or with OSError.
A pending deadline combined with startup failure returns the slot once.
Eight interrupted setups preserve all four slots, and a subsequent lookup succeeds.
IPv4/IPv6 literals bypass DNS; full capacity rejects another lookup; normal resolution and resolver failure release capacity.
Workers finish without cleanup exceptions; the previous signal handler and idle timer are restored.
regressions.counting: Count 20 table/subtest cases once. Nine named methods, eight iterations within the repeated-interruption case, assertions, before/after runs, the existing 20 deadline checks and the full-suite rerun are not additional cases.

verification.syntax: AST parsing passed for the implementation and new test file.
verification.go: No Go source changed or Go tests rerun for this validation.

primary_sources.use: Signal handlers run later in the main interpreter thread; native computation can delay their execution.
Exceptions from signal handlers can appear at arbitrary execution points, including resource-management code.
Thread.start arranges execution in a separate thread and may raise RuntimeError; capacity needs a defined owner across this handoff.

limitations: Only the proxy-owned deadline exception is deferred. This is not a guarantee of cleanup under every asynchronous exception, interpreter failure or process termination.

Exception delivery waits for the resource handoff to finish. The controlled delayed-acquire case deliberately outlasts its 20 ms timer before rejection; this is not hard real-time preemption of OS thread startup.
A resolver that never returns retains its slot, keeping abandoned resolution bounded at four. Process supervision is still needed for recovery from a permanently stuck libc resolver.
A worker admitted during the handoff may finish resolution after caller expiry, but it cannot open a destination connection or deliver an expired HTTP result.
No new Snort SID, live denial-of-service resistance, universal RFC/W3C compliance or unknown-attack prevention guarantee follows from these checks.
